divide.name: Ordered field axioms, absolute value and inequalities
divide.brief: This part covers the real numbers as an ordered field: the field axioms and the order axioms, and how familiar algebraic facts (for example 0 * a = 0, a^2 >= 0, 1 > 0, and multiplying an inequality by a negative number reverses it) follow from them. Absolute value and its properties (|ab| = |a||b|, |a| <= c exactly when -c <= a <= c), the triangle inequality and the reverse triangle inequality |(|a| - |b|)| <= |a - b|, and distance on the line. It also covers working with inequalities as proof tools: chaining and bounding estimates, the 'it suffices to show' style of argument, Bernoulli's inequality as an example, and the lemma 'if a <= b + epsilon for every epsilon > 0 then a <= b' (and its form 'if |a - b| < epsilon for every epsilon > 0 then a = b'). It notes that the rationals are also an ordered field, so nothing here yet separates the reals from the rationals. Edges: no upper bounds, supremum or completeness; those are 'Supremum, infimum and the completeness axiom'. Proof methods and quantifier handling come from 'Logic, sets and proof' and are used, not retaught. Epsilon-N estimates for sequences belong to 'Sequences'. What matters for this learner: fluency with absolute value and the triangle inequality, and the epsilon lemma, since every later epsilon proof is a chain of such estimates. Keep the axiom-level derivations to a few representative ones rather than deriving all of school algebra.

divide.name: Supremum, infimum and the completeness axiom
divide.brief: This part covers upper and lower bounds, sets bounded above, below and bounded, maximum and minimum, and the definitions of supremum (least upper bound) and infimum (greatest lower bound), with examples where the supremum is or is not attained (for example [0,1), {1 - 1/n}). The completeness (least upper bound) axiom, which makes the reals a complete ordered field, and its equivalent form for infimum (inf S = -sup(-S)). The epsilon characterisation of the supremum: u = sup S exactly when u is an upper bound and for every epsilon > 0 some s in S has s > u - epsilon, and the same for infimum. Practice in proving sup and inf statements directly from the definition: sup(A + B) = sup A + sup B, sup(cA) for c > 0 and c < 0, if A is a subset of B then sup A <= sup B, and sup and inf of sets of function values. The set {x in Q : x^2 < 2} as an example showing that the rationals are not complete, with the full proof of sqrt 2 left to the next part. A mention that the reals can be built from the rationals by Dedekind cuts or Cauchy sequences, without the construction. The extended reals, and writing sup S = +infinity when S is unbounded above, as notation only. Edges: ordered field facts, absolute value and the epsilon lemma come from 'Ordered field axioms, absolute value and inequalities'. The Archimedean property, density, square roots, nested intervals and uncountability are 'Consequences of completeness'. limsup and liminf belong to 'Sequences'. What matters for this learner: completeness is the one property that separates the reals from the rationals, and the learner must be able to prove statements about sup and inf straight from the definition, using the epsilon characterisation. Give room to worked proofs and to the scratch-work habit of proving 'upper bound' and 'least' as two separate steps.

divide.name: Consequences of completeness
divide.brief: This part covers the first theorems proved from the completeness axiom. The Archimedean property (the natural numbers are not bounded above; for every epsilon > 0 there is n with 1/n < epsilon), with the proof by contradiction from the supremum, and its use to show inf {1/n} = 0. Density of the rationals in the reals and density of the irrationals. Existence of a positive real x with x^2 = 2 (and, by the same method, n-th roots of positive numbers), proved from the supremum of {x : x^2 < 2}, together with the proof that sqrt 2 is irrational, so the rationals lack it. The nested interval property, proved directly from the supremum of the left endpoints, with examples showing that it fails for open intervals and for the rationals. Uncountability of the reals, proved either by nested intervals or by Cantor's diagonal argument with the care needed for decimal expansions such as 0.4999... = 0.5. Edges: the definitions of sup, inf and completeness come from 'Supremum, infimum and the completeness axiom'. The definition of countable sets and the diagonal argument for decimals in outline come from 'Logic, sets and proof'. 'Sequences' relates nested intervals to the monotone convergence theorem and proves Bolzano-Weierstrass. Open and closed sets and the Cantor set belong to 'Topology of the real line'. Continuity of n-th root functions belongs to 'Limits of functions and continuity'. What matters for this learner: these are model existence proofs (a number is produced as a supremum and then shown to have the property), the same pattern used later for monotone convergence, the intermediate value theorem and integrability; and the Archimedean property is the everyday tool for choosing N in later epsilon proofs.
